claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the degree of atomic-scale chemical disorder.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder modulates local lattice distortions and electron-scattering rates, which in turn control electron-pairing strength.
Processing conditions can be varied to change local compositional fluctuations while maintaining constant overall stoichiometry.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder induces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions affect the local electronic density of states.
Local lattice distortions affect electron-scattering mechanisms.
Increasing atomic-scale disorder introduces local strain fields that modify the electronic band structure.
Moderate disorder enhances electron pairing by optimizing electron-phonon coupling.
Excessive disorder increases electron-scattering rates and eventually suppresses superconductivity.
An optimized moderate level of atomic disorder will produce a higher superconducting transition temperature than the standard-processing baseline.
An optimized moderate level of atomic disorder will produce a sharper superconducting transition than the standard-processing baseline.
Very low or very high disorder will produce lower transition temperatures or broader superconducting transitions.
The standard-processing baseline has an intermediate level of atomic disorder.
The proposed relationship applies only within a bounded window of compositional disorder.
Oxygen contamination or mechanical stress may obscure the proposed disorder-superconductivity relationship.
Annealing time and cooling rate can be used to vary atomic disorder in the proposed controlled sample series.
TEM and atom-probe tomography can quantify the relevant local lattice distortions and elemental distributions.
Failure to observe the predicted non-monotonic correlation between measured disorder or lattice distortion and transition temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
